This is a game that had a TON of potential, but completely missed the mark.

I was extremely excited for all that this game promise.. This game promises No Classes, No Levels, Total Freedom of Play...the reality of the game is quite different.

I think everyone understood there was some wiggle room in their marketing statements, as there would be some type of progression and "leveling", which there is. Instead of the traditional leveling, you earn Skill Points and Ability points and apply them to a "skill wheel", which unlocks different skills for different weapons. This ultimately allows for a single character to take on any role in the game.. wanna be a tank, switch weapons, wanna be a healer, switch weapons, so the only real reason to create an "alt" is to join a different faction or for cosmetic purposes.

Unfortunately, where the game goes horribly wrong is in the forced progression curve, which winds up being far more restrictive and linear than many of the other MMORPG's I played (including SWTOR, which had a very linear and specific storyline to follow).

The usual MMO experience is you move into a zone, pick up all the quests, do the quests, gain experience "clear" the zone and then move onto the next, harder zone. Some people choose to focus on one quest at a time, some people follow a specific storyline, and some people grab everything in place and grind through quests as fast as possible... Secret World is NO DIFFERENT in set up. If you do not clear most of the zone, you will not be powerful enough to move onto the next zone. However, unlike other MMO's, Secret World restricts HOW you go through the zone and forces you to constantly backtrack in a forced time sink.

In The Secret World, you accept mission A from character A. On the way to your objective you encounter character B who requests you also to complete a task at the same place. You go to accept this new missions thinking "cool, I can kill two birds with one stone" and you get a warning window that you must "pause" quest A to accept quest B. If you choose to pause quest A and take quest B, you have to go back to character A to "unpause" quest A, leaving you to run back and forth over the same ground several times... and it isn't just character A and B, you come across character C, D, E, F and G along the way and each time you talk to them you are told you can't accept their missions without abandoning the mission you are on... Freedom of play? Why can't I get BOTH bandages and medication from the pharmacy at the same time?? No, I have to get the bandages, return them to character A, then find character D again, go back to the same pharmacy and find the medication and return it to character D and then hunt out character B who wanted water from the store which was right next to the pharmacy.

The developers have offered several conflicting excuses for this baffling limitation, everything from "memory problems on the backend" to it being a high level decision made to force you to get immersed in each mission, instead of treating characters like mission hubs. Ultimately, one honest dev admitted that if they removed the limitation it would break the progression curve and they would have to reduce the amount of experience you gained from each mission and people would complain there isn't enough content. (ie, we need to force you to run back and forth because you would progress through the game too fast if we allowed you to follow a logical progression.)

This brings me back to the main selling point... "TOTAL FREEDOM OF PLAY" If I am someone who chooses to grind quests, why is there something wrong with that? If am someone who WANTS to focus on one quest at a time, great. If I want to do 3 at a time, why am I not allowed to make that choice? They made it 100% clear in the forums that this system was NOT up for debate and would NOT be changed under any circumstances. This non-intuitive questing system made the game feel like work, rather than fun. I was looking for a game that offered more freedom of gameplay and this felt exactly the opposite.

I've been a huge Mega Man fan since I was a kid renting Mega Man 3 from a local video store. I've grown to hate Capcom over their disregard for Ithe series, so I was excited for Inafune's spiritual successor, and was eagerly awaiting Mighty No. 9's release since it was first announced. But now that I have it, I feel deeply saddened to say that this game fails to do the Blue bombers legacy justice.
I understand that my expectations for it were high, as with most Mega man fans, and that could bias my opinion of the game, but the fact is that Mighty No. 9 just.... sucks. While the graphics and performance are both pretty bad, it's the actual game play that kills this game.
The game play focuses on your ability to dash into wounded enemies to absorb them. The execution of this is so painfully bad, I don't understand how anyone could have played it and said, "Yeah, this'll work." Damaged enemies don't stop attacking once they become absorbable, meaning that you'll dash into bullet frequently. Also, the idea is that absorbing enemies will give you buffs, but this element feels half-baked at best. Temporary buffs to attack or speed seem nice, but they don't fit into the game well. The level design is pretty horrid. The levels drag on and on. Life replenishes are few and far between and the game is chock full of cheap hits and instant death. And the bosses just suck.
I wanted to love Mighty No. 9, but it seemed hell bent on me hating it. If you are a Mega Man fan, this game will break your heart. It makes Mega Man X6 seem good. Yeah.

So I have a pimax 5k, and upgraded to this 8k. And it is a noticeable upgrade in SDE and resolution. The upscaling mode works great. because if you can run the 5k, you can also run the 8kx. I've also owned other headsets: Samsung odyssey, Oculus Rift S, HP Reverb. Now I gotta say that the 8kx's FOV cannot be beat. It's the reason why i stick to pimax. However, the FOV is the only advantage. The contrast, color vibrancy is admittedly slightly, barely worse than any of my other headsets. It was actually noticeably worse actually, before the latest pitool update which allows you to adjust the backlight brightness slider. Set it to 90 and now vibrancy isn't an issue. Is the big FOV worth the double price tag and slightly less vibrant colors? You decide. But for me, it's worth it. I've tried to enjoy myself in the rift S and reverb, but I just couldn't lie to myself: the narrow fov is way more distracting than the slightly less colors of the pimax.

Also I guess I'll complain about the lenses of the pimax. they're ok, that's it. I don't know how oculus does it, but even with the rift s's lower resolution, it managed to get rid of the black void between pixels that comes naturally with low resolution. it's got an anti-aliasing film on it or something, which is what pimax needs to make it magical. But as of now, it doesn't.

Also, the cable that I got was giving me problems: I would shake it and loose the image, and the headset LED would turn red. Oddly enough, the problem went away. However, when I plug in a pair of headphones into the headphone plug, there is a very loud buzzing electrical noise in the background. It tells me that there is still something wrong with the cable. I have a workaround for the buzzing for now: plug headphones into computer output jack instead. But I worry that the rogue electrical signals could fry the headset in time.

And lastly, the default audio that comes with the pimax sucks, as it floats above your ears and sounds very nasal.

I talked to pimax customer support, and they totally ignored the audio issue I had and are only focusing on the intermittent video that I first reported. It seems like I will not be getting a replacement cable and will have to buy a new one myself. If I did not have the audio issue, I would've given it 5 stars.

I have a low-tolerance for sandbox-style games that gloss over paper-thin plots in the hope that randomly-generated encounters will make for fun gameplay. I don't have the time to wander around all day hoping to find a way around a mountain with trolls guarding it...only to be killed by wolves over and over (I'm looking at you, Skyrim and Fallout). Which is why Far Cry: New Dawn is such a pleasant surprise.

Far Cry gets right down to business with a plot that's familiar but serviceable -- you're a fixer sent to help a town get on its feet in a post-apocalyptic 2035. The train you're on is (literally) derailed by the local warlords known as the Twins (Mickey, voiced by Cara Ricketts and Lou, voiced by Leslie Miller). They attempt to forcibly recruit Thomas Rush (Patrick Garrow), who has all the skills necessary to get a community back on their feet. In the ensuing chaos, your character known only as the Captain escapes, forced to leave Rush behind with the Twins. From there, you're recruited by Carmina Rye (Reina Hardesty) to help get the teetering community of Prosperity back on its feet. But instead of peacefully helping civilians, you're recruiting for a war -- by doing favors for other locals, you hope to bring them together in a united front to defeat the Twins. If this sounds a lot like the plot of The Walking Dead (substitute "Negan" for "The Twins") you're right.

It's getting there that makes the difference. There's of course a crafting system that relies on found materials like metal parts and duct tape. There's vehicles to ride and companions to recruit with each successful mission. It's a good thing too, because Carmina is really annoying. We immediately set out to recruit an adorable dog known as Timber. You can just pet Timber, and he acts like a good dog -- but he's also a vicious killer who will tear the throat out of any bandit that opposes you. There's plenty of things to kill too, including bears with attack animations that are so realistic that it's traumatic to go experience. With a system entirely revolving around finding places to go and people to kill, the game clips along at a decent pace. If it has a flaw, it's the absurd amount of swearing, which jumps over the line from "okay, it's a rough place so people swear" to "look we can swear, FUUUUUUUUU--"

This is a game that awards casual play -- it's to jump in and out. The world is beautiful and reactive; if you stand around long enough, someone will inevitably pass you by and someone else will inevitably try to kill them. How you react is part of the fun. I had flashbacks to the adventures I enjoyed with me and my pooch in Fallout 3...a high bar, I suspect, every post-apocalyptic game has tried to achieve ever since, including the Fallout franchise itself. Far Cry: New Dawn comes pretty close, and that's high praise indeed.

To start with,
The good:
Drakensang is a beautifully rendered game. A classic RPG in the style of NWN and KoToR. It has a rich, in depth story that engages both your senses and your mind. All while delighting you visually, and keeping the action moving with the simple yet elegant interface. Lovers of KoToR will really recognize the similarities here.
I don't think I have ever heard more fitting music for a game. It suits the mood every time and helps to create a wonderful atmosphere. Sound effects and voice acting are well done as well. And finally, that brings me to the strongest part, the graphics. The graphics for this game are honestly perfect. While there may be better looking games, the balance this game achieves between being visually spectacular but not too distracting is really quite remarkable and very necessary for an RPG of this depth. This game is a real treat to play and I would highly recommend it to RPG Lovers.

The bad:
Unfortunately, this game does have it's dark side. The bugs. Mostly, they stem from trying to get the game to even boot up. Now with most games, I have come to expect some minor tweaking of both hardware and software settings to get the game to run; however, with Drakensang these tweaks become repetitive and irksome at times. First this game has a conflict with internal modems, especially those that it recognizes as a "sound modem." I don't even think my computer has a sound modem but anyway, every time I want to run the game, I have to go to control panel and disable the modem. This isn't too terrible of a conflict but it becomes a real pain as every time I want to play the game I have to do this because of course when you shut down your computer, the modem is recognized and enabled upon restart. That is a minor issue but frustrating none the less.
The most frustrating issue with this game is getting past the copy protection software at start up. The game will not start and it tells you to enter an original copy of the disc, which is funny because I have not made a copy and I only try to run the game with the original disc in the drive. I am not exaggerating when I say that there have been times when I have had to start the game 7 or 8 times before it recognizes that I am not running a bootlegged copy. While I recognize the need to safeguard against bootlegged copies of the game to ensure that the developers turn a profit, the terrible copy recognition software makes the game almost not even worth playing because it's time consuming just trying to get it to run. And as far as I know, as of this posting, there are no patches yet available that fix any of these issues. And if there are, good luck finding them because the developers have created a vicious circle bouncing you back and forth between their web sites (some of which display in German at first until you can figure out how to make it display in English), as your trying to find help.
Suffice it to say that I am not the only one having tech issues with this game as well. The web is alive with horror stories from people trying to run this game. I feel fortunate that I can get it to run 1 out of every 3 to 4 times I try to start it.

All in all, if you plan on purchasing this game be prepared to show some patience. This game is very finicky. Which is sooo! disappointing because when it runs it's a superb experience.

I just got the keyboard today and I can say for 17 dollars im pretty happy. The keys are about as loud as the come (so I wouldn't get this if you're going to use it around other people). The key wobble is also massive on large keys such as the shift key (but the space bar luckily is pretty stable). Unfortunately, I just got this and the led under my Numpad 0 was broken when I got it. The LEDs are very bright and look pretty nice. They do all sorts of effects but they are not color-changing (Each key can only be the color shown in the picture). The keyboard overall feels fairly sturdy and it is clear that the plastic is thick and durable. If your a huge stickler for keyboards I definitely wouldn't buy this one but if you are looking to game on a budget or just want to try a mechanical keyboard this is likely the perfect product for you.
